figures.caption: Figure 1: Example stimuli and regions of interest (ROIs). (A) Example trials of each presentation 2 condition in the main experiment. The four conditions differed in whether words appeared in the first and/or 3 second frame. Frame 3 always contained two false font strings. The timing and location of words was 4 counterbalanced within each condition (e.g., on one-word trials the word could be in either frame 1 or 2, on 5 the top or bottom). After frame 3, the participant had 3.65 s to make their response. (B) Examples of the 6 four stimulus categories used in the visual category-selective region localizer (words, false font strings, 7 faces, and limbs). (C) Example stimuli from the language localizer. Each real sentence consisted of 12 real 8 English words, and each jabberwocky sentence consisted of 12 pseudowords. Each (pseudo)word was 9 presented for 450 ms followed by a 50 ms blank. (D) Example ROIs in a representative subject’s inflated 10 cortical surfaces. The regions on the ventral view (top two images) were defined from the visual category 11 localizer. The white V4 region was obtained from a previous study (White et al., 2023). The pink regions on 12 the lateral view (bottom images) were defined from the language localizer. Abbreviations: FFA: fusiform 13 face area; pOTS-words: word-selective posterior occipitotemporal sulcus; mOTS-words: word-selective 14 middle occipitotemporal sulcus; mFus-words: word-selective mid-fusiform sulcus/gyrus; VTC-limbs: limb 15 area in the ventral temporal surface, extending laterally to include the extrastriate body area (EBA) in some 16 subjects; STS: superior temporal sulcus; PG: Precentral Gyrus; IFS: inferior frontal sulcus. 17

Figure 2: Effects of presentation condition on behavior and brain responses. (A) The left 4 panel shows mean task accuracy for reporting the number of words as a function of the presentation 5 condition. “2seq” means two words presented sequentially, while “2sim” means two words presented 6 simultaneously. Error bars are ± 1 SEM. Asterisks denote p-values from pairwise comparisons (***p<0.001, 7 **=p<0.01, *=p<0.05). The right panel shows the differences in accuracy across pairs of conditions. The 8 dots are individual participants, the bars are the mean differences, and the error bars are 95% bootstrapped 9 confidence intervals. (B) Correct response times as a function of presentation condition, formatted in panel 10 A. (C, D and E) Mean BOLD responses in three left ventral text-selection regions, plotted in units of percent 11 signal change (p.s.c), and formatted as in panel A. (F) Whole-cortex maps of the effect of the number of 12 words presented per trial. Colors represented t-values on the mean slope across participants, thresholded 13 for p<0.05 with false discovery rate correction across all surface nodes. There are clusters of significant 14 effect in the left inferior frontal sulcus, intraparietal sulcus, occipito-temporal sulcus and fusiform gyrus. 15

Table 1: Statistical results from linear mixed effects models of two effects: the Number of Words effect and 2 Simultaneous Suppression. The first modelled single-trial BOLD responses as a function of the number of 3 words presented (excluding two-word simultaneous trials). The second tested for a difference in BOLD 4 responses between two-word sequential and two-word simultaneous trials. We report the estimates of the 5 slope for each fixed effect (in units of percent signal change), the standard error of that slope, its 95% 6 bootstrapped confidence intervals, t-values, associated p-values corrected for multiple tests using FDR 7 correction, and Bayes Factor for each effect. N is the number of subjects in which each ROI was present. 8

Table 2: Statistical results reporting pairwise differences for the number of words effect for left hemisphere 2 text-selective regions. The third row for each ROI is a difference of differences in the first two rows. Here, 3 we report the mean differences across conditions, the standard error, 95% bootstrapped confidence 4 intervals, t-values, associated p-values corrected for multiple tests using FDR correction and Bayes Factor 5 for each comparison. 6

Figure 5: Lexical frequency effects on responses to two words in text-selective regions. (A) 2 Behavioral results as a function of presentation condition and lexical frequency. “2-seq” means two words 3 presented sequentially, “2-sim” means two words presented simultaneously. Filled bars are for trials with 4 two high-frequency words, empty bars are for trials with two low-frequency words. (B) Average responses 5 in text-selective ventral regions. Error bars are ± 1 SEM. F indicates a significant main effect of lexical 6 frequency. The asterisks indicate: ***=p<0.001, **=p<0.01, *=p<0.05. 7

Figure 6: Two models that can explain the effects of the lexical frequency of word pairs in the 7 sequential and simultaneous trials. Within each row, the first two panels show neuronal activation over time, 8 as a form of evidence accumulation towards a word identification threshold. For both models, the threshold 9 for low-frequency words is higher than for high-frequency words. We assume that on each trial either two 10 low-frequency words are presented, or two high-frequency words are presented. The rightmost panels show 11 the predicted BOLD responses, which are calculated as the integral of activation across time for each 12 condition. Both models predict smaller effects of lexical frequency in the sequential condition than the 13 simultaneous condition, as we observed empirically (Figure 5B). (A) Serial model: each word is processed 14 one at a time. On simultaneous trials, the second word starts producing activation only after the first reaches 15 its threshold, and the second word may not reach its threshold, which explains the behavioral deficit. (B) 16 Limited-capacity parallel model: On simultaneous presentation trials, both words are processed 17 simultaneously but with a shallower slope of activation over time than on sequential trials. 18

Figure 7: Schematic of a hybrid parallel-then-serial model for the processing of two simultaneously 2 presented words. The logic of this graph is similar to the models in Figure 6 that are explained in the Results 3 section, except that it does not assume processing is interrupted by a post-mask; hence this figure shows 4 both words reaching the threshold for lexical access. 5
